title: The Cosmologist: Uneven Self-Similarity in Prelude and Fugue No.9, Book I
content_blocks: I’ve gotten better, over the two and a half months that I’ve been writing this blog, at not being overly technical. It’s for this reason that I’ve been putting off talking about this prelude-and-fugue pair, because it could get really technical really fast.

So let’s begin with this.  In western music, there are twelves notes per octave.  Music that is in a traditional key (like C-major, for instance), uses only seven notes out of the twelve at any given time, with that same pattern of note repeating every octave.  Later and later in the 19th century, though, composers used more and more of those twelve notes, to the point in the 20th century where Arnold Schoenberg (among others) decided that it made sense to use all twelve tones more-or-less equally.  To give structure to this musical world of pure equality, he would use a row (a series) of twelve tones.  Different twelve-tone rows have different properties and characteristics.

Fast forward to the third quarter of the twentieth century. Another composer, Pohlman Mallalieu, discovered a group of four rows that are uniquely and thoroughly “self-similar.” Specifically, starting on the second note of the row and playing every other note produces the exact same melodic pattern as starting on the first note and playing every note in turn. This is also true starting on the third note and playing every third note, starting on the fourth note and playing every fourth note, etc. Remember that the universe of notes that this row structures is twelve notes per octave, repeating every octave.

Now, my pair of pieces is not twelve-tone, but the expanding and contracting pattern of notes used as the mode for this piece (the same used for Nos. 2 and 4 of Book I) generates a total of twelve notes spread out over two octaves. So, this, then is my universe of twelve-tones: almost all of the twelve different notes in the regular twelve tone universe, but with one doubled and one missing, spread unevenly over two-octave spans.

To this irregular, uneven twelve-tone universe I applied one of the four Mallalieu rows, generating the possibility of endless self-similarity—or “fractals.” I have already expressed my appreciation of fractals (see “Mechanical Motion,” July 11); as with Prelude No.4 from Book II, in this Fugue the fractals display themselves at different rates of motion. Since the notes are spread out unevenly, though, the self-similarity generated is one of scale degree (the scalar pattern seen), but not of interval size—in other words, we have the same sort of diatonic answers discussed in many of the earlier in this blog posts.

How can we hear which notes are part of which line? The most important feature is the range, whether higher or lower, but the rate of motion is also a clue. In the combined video of Michael playing these pieces I provide visual cues as well: each fractal line is associated with a particular position on the screen, and each note is visually cued by a flash in the brightness of that portion of the screen. At it’s peak, with five lines going on simultaneously, one is heard every two beats, one every three, one every four, one every five, and the fastest, in the center, every half beat.

Well, at least, that’s what happens in the second half of the Fugue, starting about 2:09 into the video. The Prelude presents not the row but this particular twelve-tone universe, going through them like a circle of fifths (that is, playing every fifth note, in order). The Fugue (at 1:27 into the video) starts by treating the row as a skeleton, filling in those notes with other, faster notes. A more-or-less standard sounding fugue unfolds with that filled-in subject, but slowly shedding the shorter filling-in notes, until the final, five-level fractal fugue section referred to above.

Whew!  Did your eyes glaze over?  I do apologize!  So now let me talk about the name of this pair—The Cosmologist.  Just as the universe spins out in similar ways but, at different rates of speed and spin, creating an infinity of shapes and appearances, so too these notes spin out over the vast expanse of its tonal universe, creating an infinity of shapes and sounds even while expressing the same basic shape in its fractal multiplicity.  Put another way…enjoy!
